title: A coming age of leisure is a dangerous myth
subtitle: AI will take our jobs, but it won't give us more free time
author: Adrian Johnston
introduction: Over 200 economists and tech insiders, including 16 Nobel Prize winners, signed an open letter this month, warning that AI may take our jobs. Some, like Bill Gates, argue that this is a good thing, and that AI can usher in an age of leisure. But Adrian Johnston, praised as “one of the most audacious philosophers writing today” and hailed by Slavoj Žižek as our generation’s Herbert Marcuse, argues here that this idea is a dangerous myth. True leisure, he contends, must be shaped by forces that differ from those shaping work and profit-production. Yet the business models of tech companies rely on them having precise, fine-grained control over our “free” time, turning us into producers of content, attention and, increasingly, training data. AI may take our jobs, but it will not compensate us with more free time.
body:
The smartphone is surely the iconic commodity of early-twenty-first-century capitalism. We use smartphones as our alarm clocks. We check the weather, social media, our e-mails, text messages, calendar appointments, to-do lists, and so on, as soon as we wake up and shut off the alarm. Our phones keep us up to date with the news. We shop and listen to music with them. We navigate with them. They monitor our health. These devices, and the information technology that enables them, have become essential for organizing, coordinating, and discharging both our professional and familial obligations, as well as for socializing. After the day’s work is done, we entertain ourselves with these hand-held, portable screens, watching, playing, liking, commenting, flirting, gambling, and so on. We constantly stare at them, in bed, while standing around, when alone, when with others, on transportation, on the toilet—wherever, whenever.

Among the many changes in our lives inaugurated by new information technologies, some of the most radical are changes in how we work. Old jobs are disappearing or being rendered unrecognizable. Established and new professions alike are being threatened with disappearance by the rise of so-called artificial intelligence.

We confuse working uncompensated for others with playing around on our devices for our own first-personal amusement and distraction.

We may quickly be approaching a fork in the road between, as Friedrich Engels and Rosa Luxemburg put it well over a century ago, socialism or barbarism. If and when the combined forces of AI, robotics, and other forms of automation bring about the much-feared “jobs apocalypse”—under capitalism, the prospect of IT liberating us from drudgery sadly manifests instead as the threat of homelessness and starvation—a load-bearing pillar of the social contract for the majority of people in capitalist societies, that one must work to eat, will become untenable. What happens then? Do we accept the vast majority of humanity, once made redundant as laborers by IT, being condemned to poverty and death? Or, do we forge a novel social contract in which being employed no longer determines one’s worthiness to eat? Will it be barbarism or socialism indeed?

Such questions aside for the moment, both labor and leisure have been, and continue to be, significantly reshaped by smartphones and the IT from which they are inseparable. However, in the rest of what follows, I want to focus specifically on a certain fashion in which the very relationship between labor and leisure has been profoundly and insidiously altered within the information-technology capitalism of the twenty-first century. It is not just that the unfree time of mandatory labor for others increasingly seeps into the free time of voluntary leisure for oneself—as when I find myself reluctantly or unintentionally performing unpaid overtime for my employer by using my iPhone to keep up with work e-mails outside my normal working hours.

The economic cycle involves production, distribution, exchange, and consumption. We tend to see the first three of these categories as the more social and public sides of economic life, involving the shared spaces of workplaces and marketplaces (predominantly shaped by a combination of potent corporate and government interests). By contrast, we tend to think of the fourth category, consumption, as primarily asocial and private. Once I purchase a product, the story goes, I withdraw it from the noisy hustle and bustle of both the workplace and the marketplace. Perhaps I take it home to enjoy on my own in my spare time as I see fit. When I am consuming, I often take myself to be neither socially producing nor publicly exchanging. But this is a mistake.

All commodities move through the stages of production, distribution, exchange, and consumption. But when the smartphone goes on this journey, it undermines the distinction between production and consumption, the two extreme poles. What is more, it does so in ways that, at least for the time being, super-charge capitalism, rather than bring about the end of capital’s reign with the purported transition to a neo/techno-feudalism (with the monopolists of Big Tech as our new landed aristocracy).

With the mid-twentieth-century rise of consumer capitalism, our free time was colonized by capital and harnessed as yet another source of profits through the commodification of leisure activities (hobbies, sports, games, and the like) and their instruments and accoutrements—and, along with this came the ever more insistent intrusions of advertising, marketing, and the like into our private lives. In the workplace, the site of production, workers produce surplus value for their capitalist employers, by producing more value than they are paid in wages. While off the clock in the marketplace, the site of exchange, workers produce more surplus-value for other capitalists by buying various commodities. But, before the invention of smartphones and the rise of information-technology capitalism, once the worker retreated from the spheres of production and exchange into the apparently private spheres of consumption, they could be taken, albeit erroneously, to be finally in the secluded domestic domain of rest and relaxation, at last enjoying free time in ways that contribute directly neither to capital’s productivity nor profitability.

Smartphones and the applications that run on them turn their purchasers not only into consumers, but also into unwitting and unpaid laborers qua producers. Every time I consume contemporary technological commodities, by interacting with smartphones, tablets, laptops, desktops, or any other internet-connected devices (including my car) in an ever-growing “Internet of Things,” I produce completely gratis for various IT capitalists valuable commodities: steady quantities of vendable data, for which I am paid nothing, as well as improvements to the same algorithms I simultaneously am paying to utilize as a consumer. I am being sold back the virtually commodified leisure activities I myself (and others like me) at the same time contribute unremunerated to producing.

Not only do the IT capitalists not pay us a single cent for either the data or the better-trained algorithms we produce for them through our consumption of IT commodities, we actually pay for the privilege of being thus exploited, forking over our hard-earned cash for smartphones, apps, memory storage, online subscriptions, streaming services, and so on. In relation to today’s Big-Tech version of monopoly capitalism, we are not “cloud serfs” of neo-feudal IT lords hovering virtually above the lowly gig-worker peasantry. We are, rather, fully unpaid IT (lumpen)proletarians who even help pay for the IT bourgeoisie’s means of production out of our own pockets, all the while borrowing at usurious rates from financial capitalists to do so. Likewise, privatized AI promises to turn what Karl Marx describes as our collectively generated “general intellect,” our intellectual and ideational commons, into the living, embodied apogee, the maximal intensification, of the capitalism-inherent contradiction between socialized production and private property.

This perverse high-tech convergence of leisurely consumption with laborious production is what we nowadays all-too-often misidentify as our “free time.” In this misidentification, we confuse working uncompensated for others with playing around on our devices for our own first-personal amusement and distraction. The true sense of the adjective “free” in this IT-capitalist sort of “free time” is that we let our now-techno-scientifically-mediated leisure time be transubstantiated into absolutely unpaid labor time for, as Slavoj Žižek might put it, less than nothing. That is to say, we are paid nothing to produce the same commodity we pay its owner to consume. To paraphrase Žižek, such unfree expenditures of labor time disguised as the leisure of free time would be our “less-than-free time.” These temporal expenditures and their fruits are being stolen right out from under our noses, minute-by-minute and click-by-click. All the while, we happily pay to be robbed.

SUGGESTED READING A post-work world would be a solipsistic nightmare By B. Scot Rousse

This IT-capitalist loop of self-reinforcing absolute exploitation is one of the most vicious of the various vicious circles of our times. We increasingly lose our freedom in letting our free time become free-as-entirely-unpaid laboring time, further empowering the capitalists vacuuming up the value created by this “free” time. Our less-than-free time is a source not only of pure profit, but of ex nihilo and uncut surplus-value for our exploiters. Having untold legions of unpaid workers, who do not even know that they are working for you because they misrecognize their maximal exploitation as their minimal margin of freedom, is the ultimate capitalist dream-come-true. It amounts to, in Herbert Marcuse’s words, a “repressive desublimation” of Marx’s communist dream of workers-in-solidarity consciously and rationally transubstantiating labor into leisure—this vision is on display in the Marxian corpus starting with such early texts as the 1844 Paris Economic and Philosophical Manuscripts—into a capitalist dream of workers-in-isolation (staring solo at their screens) unconsciously and irrationally allowing their leisure to be transubstantiated into maximally-alienated labor as productive of maximum surplus-value expropriated for less than nothing by a tiny cabal of self-styled tech titans.

Maybe this pinnacle is also a tipping point, with the present triumph of the oligarchs of Big Tech marking the beginning of the end of not only neoliberalism, but capitalism itself. Perhaps a far-right, high-tech monopoly capitalism turbo-charged by 100% pure surplus-value will somehow burn itself out before it literally burns away the planet’s delicate ecosystems. It would not be impossible for something on the order of the so-called “singularity” of the advent of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), a queryable self-reflexive form of the general intellect, to replace the capitalist social contract of labor-for-food with something much better, rather than something much worse.

My utopian fantasy along these lines, in which I admittedly place scant faith, can be summed up through combining the titles of a 1984 American anti-communist movie and a famous (and roughly contemporaneous) Hollywood film franchise: Terminator: Red Dawn. What if AGI, drawing on our own general intellect, concludes that Marxism really does formulate the most cogent account of human social history available, and consequently takes over our collective lives so as to impose upon us a radically egalitarian communism of techno-scientifically-produced relative abundance for our own good? That might be nice.

To come to a close, the mundane smartphone can be seen as a subtle-but-hideous combination of two monstrosities envisioned by the French psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan. These monstrosities are designated by two of Lacan’s numerous neologisms: “lamella” and “lathouse.” The lamella, introduced in Seminar XI of 1964, is one’s repressed libido in the guise of an ultra-thin, manta-ray-like creature that slips under one’s closed door at night and slides itself over one’s sleeping face. The lathouse, introduced in Seminar XVII of 1969-70, is a techno-gadget toy that comes to bend desire around itself: a commodified attractor point, here an IT-capitalist objet petit a, for subjects’ libidinal economies as backed by what John Maynard Keynes christens “effective demand.”

As hybrid lamellae-lathouses, the screens of our “smart” devices are slick, flat surfaces that hug our faces. These sneakiest of face-huggers (to invoke imagery from the Alien film franchise resonant with the Lacanian myth of the lamella) drain our time and energy, disempowering us while feeding us the illusion that our self-constructed virtual prisons are our other-given spaces of freedom. What these face-huggers suck out of us, siphoning straight into the ever-deeper pockets of our IT masters as contemporary monopoly capitalists, is what Lacan calls “surplus enjoyment” (plus-de-jouir). Our IT-mediated surplus enjoyment is our leisure-become-labor time as uncut surplus-value, pure profit for exploitative others. In our current circumstances, the more of our free time we spend scrolling, the less free we become.
